title: Feel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fiction

paragraphs.en: Every summer, we long for a much-needed break from daily life, dreaming of self-reinvention in some distant paradise. But really, holidays can be absolute hell. Instead of relaxation we encounter heaving crowds, lumpy beds, the caprices of our loved ones and the grim truth that we can escape neither their worst failings nor our own, however far we travel.

Small wonder, then, that the disaster holiday has become a booming subgenre in fiction. For most of us, the levels of luxury promised by hit TV series The White Lotus are pure fantasy, yet we’re all vulnerable to the expensive promises we’ve been sold. Two of the smartest offerings in fiction this summer come from Claire Powell’s All In and Chloë Ashby’s Family Friends. In the former, a struggling couple whose marriage is on the rocks go on an all-inclusive Spanish weekend break, paid for by a rich brother. Poignant and extremely funny, the frictions that ensue are all too believable.

So, too, is the implosion of Ashby’s group of friends who have a decades-long custom of holidaying together in the south of France. This year, however, their marriages are threatened by one husband’s deceit, the lingering attraction between old friends and the arrival of a vivacious teenage stepdaughter. Poised and gripping, it uses a sweltering Mediterranean setting to amp up tensions to dramatic effect.

In Sabine Durrant’s superb thriller Dead Heat, meanwhile, a failed journalist, his more successful media friend and a former school contemporary, now a Gatsbyesque billionaire, find their Greek adventure transformed not only into a shameful reminder of racism in their shared past, but something outright murderous. Being thrown together to brave blazing summer heat only intensifies existing tensions as Durrant expertly brings the drama to a head.

Many characters seeking escape find that a change of scene only makes problems worse. Deborah Levy’s Hot Milk , adapted as a film last year by Rebecca Lenkiewicz, chronicles a family unravelling in a Spanish fishing village. Rose pays thousands to a clinic to cure her mysterious paralysis while Sofia distracts herself with local beauty, Ingrid, as unresolved conflicts between mother and daughter start to boil over.

A fateful holiday also inspires the scathing, semi-autobiographical play in Jo Hamya’s novel The Hypocrite . Sophia is taken out of school to act as her novelist father’s amanuensis, though he spends much of his time in Sicily seducing local women instead of bonding with his daughter. Years later, he is appalled to see that Sophia has adapted his parenting failures for the stage, though the novel cleverly hints at aspects of her own behaviour on that holiday which Sophia may have conveniently chosen to forget.

The fancier the surroundings, the worse a fictional holiday is likely to be. In William Rayfet Hunter’s Sunstruck , an invitation to his university friend Lily’s parents’ chateau is the catalyst for unwelcome epiphanies about the class and race differences between the narrator and Lily’s family, even as he becomes involved with her wayward brother. Lucy Foley’s The Midnight Feast also plays with this trope to great effect, when the opening weekend of a high-end wellness retreat in the West Country is disrupted by revelations from a guest’s disastrous stay many years before.

Our attempts to get away from it all can often lead us right back to what we left home to avoid. In Deepa Anappara’s ambitious, multilayered The Last of Earth , Victorian adventurer Katherine hopes her journey into the forbidden kingdom of Tibet will help her overcome difficult feelings about her heritage. Unfortunately, disguising herself as a male pilgrim to cross dangerous unknown terrain only serves to underline Katherine’s alienation as she attempts to become the first European woman to reach Lhasa.
